name: Aisha Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I've been the senior buyer for groceries and drinks at Delgado and Sons Wholesale for twenty-eight years. It's a family firm that supplies corner shops, cafes and church halls from a cash-and-carry depot. I start at seven with a cup of tea and the order book, a real book, because I trust my own handwriting. I ring the suppliers, walk the aisles with the warehouse lads, and by afternoon I'm often on the phone with a shopkeeper whose delivery is late.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about the job, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: What I love is that people rely on me. A small shop opens at six because I got the milk and bread right. What wears me out is the hours on my feet and the new rules head office keeps adding. My husband Rafael has an upholstery workshop, and he says I treat the depot like another child.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. I call this one "AI Plateau". If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I've heard it before, and the shops still need milk and bread. At work I'd say keep doing it right and ignore the fashions. To my friends at church I'd say it's just another gadget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm relieved, but I'm not at ease. Old Mr Delgado is 80, and his son Tomás has talked about selling to a bigger group. If that happens, new people arrive with new systems, and I might be asked to leave at 60. That's my worry, not AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I do. I'd keep my paper order book and my calls, I'd keep up the monthly shift at the church food bank, and keep paying into the pension. I'd also talk to Rafael about whether we should pay down the last of the mortgage a bit faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I like my work and I'm good at it, but I can see old firms going. It's just not what I want in my last years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said uneasy, even if little changes. What's on your mind at Delgado's?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I trained as a buyer when it was all relationships. Machines can count, but they cannot know that Mrs Okafor's shop will never sell a particular brand because her customers distrust it. If it ever were useful, I'd try it, but nobody has shown me it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your faith or community say to you about a future like this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My faith teaches me to do the work in front of me and trust that I'll be looked after. It doesn't mean I sit and wait. I'd pray, and I'd also check the pension papers.

say: I'd say I've **heard it before**, and the shops still need milk and bread.
To friends at church I'd say it's just another gadget.
think: Privately my worry is not AI but the owner's son selling Delgado's, with new people and **new systems**.
At 60 I might be **asked to leave**.
do: Keep my **paper order book** and supplier calls, and my monthly food bank shift.
Talk to Rafael about paying the last of the **mortgage** faster.
feel: **Uneasy**: I like my work, but old firms like ours are going.
S0.quote: Machines can count, but they cannot know that Mrs Okafor's shop will never sell a particular brand because her customers distrust it.
fieldNote: Her **unease** comes from the family firm's possible sale, not from AI.
Trusts handwriting and personal knowledge of each shop.
Faith and practicality sit side by side: pray and check the pension papers.

steps.text: Keep the paper order book and daily supplier calls
Pay down the last of the mortgage faster
Keep the monthly shift at the church food bank

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. I call this one "Steady Disruption". If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's see it prove itself. At work I'd say we can't lose the personal touch with shopkeepers. To friends I'd say a country should look after people who work hard and still have to learn new things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, the reorder lists could go to software. It's most of what my junior buyers do, and a good part of what I do. If the owners are tempted to cut, I'm worried about the young people, like Fatima, who've only just got a mortgage. Me, I think I'd last the longest, but the family may sell before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in my place and watch carefully. I'd speak up for the younger ones at the owners' table, and I'd make sure they know how to speak to shopkeepers. I'd save more each month in case things change faster, and I'd put off the new kitchen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not for tomorrow, but I have a feeling the old way of doing business is slipping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your tasks might a computer system take first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The reorder lists, the price comparisons, the booking of delivery slots. My calls to shopkeepers would be last, because they're not about numbers, they're about trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who should help the staff if the depot changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our community, our church, and the owners themselves. I wouldn't expect the government to do everything, but a state apprenticeship scheme for people to retrain would be right. Work gives people dignity, handouts don't.

say: I'd say let's **see it prove itself**, and we can't lose the personal touch with shopkeepers.
To friends I'd say people who work hard deserve help **learning** the new things.
think: Privately reorder lists could go to software, and that's most of what the **junior buyers** do.
I worry for Fatima, who just took a **mortgage**.
do: Speak up for the younger buyers at the **owners' table** and keep teaching them to talk to shopkeepers.
Save more each month and put off the new **kitchen**.
feel: **Anxious**: it's not for tomorrow, but the old way of doing business feels like it's slipping.
S1.quote: My calls to shopkeepers would be last, because they're not about numbers, they're about trust.
fieldNote: Values work and apprenticeships over handouts, in line with her traditional outlook.
Anxiety is slow, tied to a feeling that her style of business is slipping.

steps.text: Speak up for the junior buyers at the owners' table
Save more each month and postpone the new kitchen
Teach the juniors to talk with shopkeepers face to face

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. I call this one "AGI by 2028". If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and God help us. At work I'd tell the staff we'll stand together. To friends I'd say we need to look after our own, with work and family first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think the depot's buying goes to machines. A smart system could order better than me, and cheaper. I'm 58, I have never used these tools, and I'm too old to learn from scratch. I'd feel I'd failed, even though it isn't my fault.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd first sit down with Rafael and count what we have. We'd stop all the extras, such as the holiday to see my sister. I'd ask the Delgados for early retirement at 60, with a fair pension. And I'd lean on my church and my children, because that's what community is for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd feel like the ground has gone. I'd pray more, and I'd not sleep much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If your job went in two years, who would you lean on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First Rafael, who's steady as a rock. Then Lucia and Mateo, who will help if it comes to that. Then the church. I'd rather not rely on the government, but if there was a decent scheme I wouldn't be proud about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with Rafael's workshop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: His workshop is made of hands. People need chairs mended, sofas recovered. It's slow, but it's real. I'd help him with his books, which I've done for years, and perhaps take on the orders and the website for him. That's something I could do.

say: I'd say it's **too fast**, God help us, and we should look after our own.
To the staff I'd say we'll **stand together**.
think: Privately depot buying goes to machines, and I'm too old to learn from **scratch**.
I'd feel I had **failed**, even though it isn't my fault.
do: Count what we have with Rafael, stop **extras** like the holiday to see my sister.
Ask the Delgados for **retirement at 60** and lean on my church and children.
feel: **Alarmed**: the ground has gone, and I'd pray more and sleep less.
S2.quote: I'd feel I'd failed, even though it isn't my fault.
fieldNote: The **alarm** is moral as much as financial: she would feel she had failed.
Turns first to husband, children and church.
Would help Rafael with the books and orders in his upholstery workshop.

steps.text: Count savings with Rafael and cancel the holiday to my sister
Ask the Delgados for early retirement at 60 with fair pension
Lean on the church and my children for support
Take over the books and orders for Rafael's workshop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. I call this one "AGI by 2031". If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have time, and we should use it well. At work I'd say train the young. At church I'd say we must prepare our children and not wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel a bit safer. I'd be 63, which is the age when I'd planned to stop. I'd also have the pension. My worry would be Lucia and Mateo and their kids, if they have any.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work until 62 and prepare a handover for Fatima, who's the best of the juniors. I'd save more, and pay the mortgage down with a lump sum. And I'd encourage Mateo to keep up his electrician trade, because wiring and fuses will stay human for a good while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steadier. I'd say it's like knowing the weather will turn, so you bring a coat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years instead of two. What's different for you and for your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn a trade or a craft, and to be reliable. Everything else can be learned. A person who turns up, keeps their word and works hard will always find a place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell young people about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like to think the community would step up. We can run a Saturday club for teenagers to learn skills with their hands, and an evening class on the new machines for older people like me. It's what a church hall is for.

say: I'd say we have time and should **use it well**, training the young.
At church I'd say we must prepare our children and not wait.
think: Privately I feel **safer**, as I'd be 63, when I planned to stop.
My worry is **Lucia and Mateo** and their children.
do: Work until **62** and prepare a handover for Fatima.
Pay the **mortgage** down with a lump sum and keep Mateo in his electrician trade.
feel: **Anxious**, but steadier, like knowing the weather will turn so you bring a coat.
S3.quote: A person who turns up, keeps their word and works hard will always find a place.
fieldNote: Five years brings her **steadiness** and a handover plan.
She wants the church hall used for hands-on classes for teenagers.
She trusts character over credentials, and wants the church hall used for practical learning.

steps.text: Work until 62 and hand over to Fatima
Pay the mortgage down with a lump sum
Encourage Mateo to stay in his electrician trade
Help run a Saturday skills club at the church hall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. I call this one "AGI by 2036". If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's plenty of time, so let's be sensible. At work I'd say keep the standards. To friends I'd say pray, work and plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it hardly touches me. I'd be retired and probably a grandmother. I'd be sad for the old firm if it changed beyond recognition. But I'd say it's the next generation's turn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work until 63, perhaps stay on part-time to teach Fatima, then retire. I'd use some savings to help Lucia and Mateo get a house. And I'd put a small amount to help Rafael buy a new sewing machine for his shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but only gently. I'd say it's like watching rain from inside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years takes you well past retirement. What stays with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them work is a blessing, family is the first thing, and you shouldn't be too proud to ask for help. And to save, a little, always. I learned that from my mother, who never had much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you pass on to your own children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Perhaps a bit of sadness that the old ways of doing business, a handshake and a name, may go. But sadness is not fear. I've had a good run, and I'd like the young ones to have one too.

say: I'd say there's plenty of time, so **be sensible** and keep the standards at work.
To friends I'd say **pray, work and plan** for the next generation.
think: Privately it hardly touches me: I'd be **retired**, probably a grandmother.
I'd be sad if the old firm changed beyond recognition.
do: Work to **63**, perhaps part-time to teach Fatima, then retire.
Help Lucia and Mateo with a **house** and buy Rafael a new sewing machine.
feel: **Uneasy**, but gently, like watching rain from inside.
S4.quote: Work is a blessing, family is the first thing, and you shouldn't be too proud to ask for help.
fieldNote: The **distance** leaves sadness more than fear.
Her advice is rooted in her mother's frugality and faith.
Money goes to the next generation's home, her chosen use of savings.

steps.text: Work to 63, part-time at the end to teach Fatima
Help Lucia and Mateo toward a house deposit
Buy Rafael a new sewing machine for the workshop

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year picture worries me most, because I'd have no time to hand things over properly or to see my children settled. What would help is notice, a fair pension, and a proper apprenticeship scheme for people to learn new work. And decent owners who treat people as people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd say not everyone who avoids new tools is foolish. Some of us have simply watched what happens when a firm forgets its people. I'd like to be asked what I know before I'm replaced.

headlineQuote: Not everyone who avoids new tools is foolish. Some of us have simply watched what happens when a firm forgets its people.
portrait: Aisha is a **58-year-old** senior buyer of groceries and drinks at a family wholesaler serving corner shops, cafes and church halls.
She is a traditional, church-going woman who never uses **AI tools** and trusts her paper order book and her calls.
Her mood climbs from uneasy to **alarmed** as the timeline shortens; she fears the firm's sale and feeling a failure.
She blames distant owners and cold systems, favours work and apprenticeships over handouts, and leans on family and church.
Savings and a husband's **upholstery workshop** give her options, including taking over his books and orders.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries her most, leaving no time to hand over or see her children settled.
whatWouldHelp: Notice, a fair **pension**, a real apprenticeship scheme and decent owners who treat people as people.
